entities.name: Richard von Greiffenklau zu Vollrads
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Richard von Greiffenklau zu Vollrads, who served as Archbishop and Elector of Trier from 1511 until his death on March 23, 1531, was a pivotal figure in the Holy Roman Empire during the tumultuous dawn of the Reformation. Hailing from a prominent Rhenish noble family, his tenure coincided with the initial challenges to Catholic orthodoxy posed by Martin Luther, the political instability of the Knights' War, and the critical imperial election of Charles V. As one of the three ecclesiastical prince-electors, his strategic position along the Rhine River and his vote in imperial elections granted him considerable influence over the political and religious trajectory of Western Europe.

Elected Archbishop of Trier in 1511, Greiffenklau quickly established himself as a staunch defender of traditional Catholic doctrine and imperial authority. He played a significant role in the 1519 Imperial Election, casting his vote for Charles V, whose subsequent reign would profoundly shape European history. During the Diet of Worms in 1521, he was present when Martin Luther refused to recant his teachings, firmly aligning himself with the imperial and papal condemnation of Luther. His military prowess was tested during the Knights' War (1522–1523), where he led a coalition of Rhenish princes against the rebellious knight Franz von Sickingen, successfully besieging Sickingen's stronghold at Landstuhl and ending his challenge to princely power.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Richard von Greiffenklau zu Vollrads was a key figure in regional German history, whose decisive actions as Elector of Trier prevented the early spread of Protestantism in his territories and contributed to the consolidation of princely power during the Knights' War.
